summary: Teaches fractions of a discrete set by treating the whole SET as the '1': the denominator tells how many equal groups to share the objects into, and the numerator tells how many groups to take. 1/4 of 12 means share 12 into 4 equal groups of 3 and take one group (3); 3/4 of 12 means take three groups (9). Because the whole is the set, the same fraction gives a different count for a different-sized set (1/4 of 12 = 3, but 1/4 of 8 = 2). Also targets naming a coloured part part-to-whole (3/12), not part-to-part (3/9).
misconceptions: Takes the denominator as the answer: 1/4 of 12 is '4' because the fraction has a 4
For a non-unit fraction, finds 1/4 (=3) and stops, giving 3 for 3/4 instead of 9
Names a coloured set part-to-part (3 coloured, 9 not → 3/9) instead of part-to-whole (3/12)
Divides by the numerator instead of the denominator

activities.title: Share the set into equal groups, then take some
steps: Start with 12 counters and the request 'show me 1/4'. Set the denominator to 4 and form four group-rings (or draw four rings/circles on paper).
Deal the 12 counters out one at a time so each ring holds an equal share — 3 each. If any group is unequal, keep dealing until they match.
Take one group for 1/4: say and record '1/4 of 12 = 3'.
For 3/4, light up / shade / move three of the four groups and count 3 + 3 + 3 = 9; record '3/4 of 12 = 9'.
Change the set size: re-share 8 counters into four equal groups and see each group is now 2, so 1/4 of 8 = 2. Compare with 1/4 of 12 = 3.
State in words why 1/4 means making 4 equal groups rather than just taking 4 counters.
activities.insight: The whole is the whole SET; the denominator counts the equal groups to make and the numerator counts the groups to take. The same fraction names a different quantity when the set changes, so a fraction is a relationship, not a fixed number of objects.

activities.title: Name the coloured fraction of a set — part to whole
steps: Look at a set of 12 counters with 3 coloured. Decide what fraction is coloured.
Count the coloured objects (3) and then count the WHOLE set (all 12), not the uncoloured ones.
Explain why it is 3/12 and not 3/9: the denominator is the whole set, not the leftover uncoloured counters.
Say the fraction by name ('three twelfths') rather than 'three over twelve'.
activities.insight: Naming a fraction of a set is part-to-whole: compare the coloured objects to the whole set, not to the uncoloured remainder.

activities.title: Predict before you re-share
steps: Share 12 counters and establish that 1/4 of 12 is 3.
BEFORE sharing again, predict: 'What will 1/4 of these 8 counters be — the same 3, or different?' Give a reason.
Now share the 8 into four equal groups — 2 each — and compare the observed 2 with the prediction.
Answer follow-up prompts: Is someone right that '1/4 of 12 is 4 because there is a 4 in the fraction'? For 3/4 of 12, how many of the four groups of 3 do you take, and why three?
Explain in your own words why 1/4 means making 4 equal groups, not just taking 4 counters.
activities.insight: A child who thinks a fraction names a fixed number predicts 3 for 1/4 of 8; sharing reveals 2, refuting the 'fixed count' idea and showing 1/4 is a relationship to whatever the whole set is.

checkQuestion: Here are 12 counters. Show me 1/4 of them, and then 3/4 of them. Then tell me: why does finding 1/4 mean making 4 equal groups, rather than just taking 4 counters?
checkAnswer: 1/4 of 12 = 3 (share into 4 equal groups of 3, take one group); 3/4 of 12 = 9 (take three of the four groups). The denominator 4 says how many equal groups to make; the numerator says how many groups to take — 4 is the number of groups, not the number of counters.
